doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Jon Hendricks and Evolution of the Blues
summary: He worked with Jon Hendricks in Evolution of the Blues and describes the dancers' strike and Jon's stage presence.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Well I see one of my other favorite people on here and that is Jon Hendricks.

Oh boy, yeah. Now Jon Hendricks is a true living genius. I worked with Jon in “Evolution of the Blues,” that was in the seventies also. And I’ll never forget one episode with Jon, there was some kind of tension between the dancers and Jon and whatever, anyway it ended up I sort of sided with the dancers. And Jon, it was sort of like a walk- out. And there was like a musician/dancer strike, like that. So we said we weren’t going to do the show until certain demands were met. Jon said, “Well I’ll do the show myself.” So I said oh I’ve got to see this. So I go to see the show myself. Jon did “Evolution of the Blues” all just about solo. And killed it. It was just wonderful. It really was. I mean he is such a genius. And you know — I don’t know, have you ever seen him on stage? There’s something about his face. He has a perfect stage presence. And he’s totally focused. I mean I’ve watched this man a lot of times and he is totally focused. And just this energy exudes from him, even when he’s scatting. He’s probably only scat singing that you can really understand most of the time, and he mouths, it’s not just baloney sounds, he pays attention to the chord structure of his tones. He’s just amazing. But his diction and his timing on everything, and I mean he is like an amazing person. I just can’t —.
Yeah. He’s very articulate and spiritual.
A total character. He’s a wild man. Maybe he’s a little calmer these days, but he’s very excited. He loves jazz man. And you can tell the people that really love this music. They just exude it.
